lesson.title: Phrasal Verb Mirrors
lesson.subtitle: Fifteen separable verbs matched to their phrasal twins

hook.title: The Mirror Wall
hook.content: Fifteen frames on the mirror wall — every separable verb you own beside its phrasal twin. aufwachen / wake up. zurückkommen / come back. mitnehmen / take along. einschlafen / fall asleep. aufstehen / get up. aufmachen / open (up!). zumachen / shut (to-close!). anmachen / turn on. aussuchen / pick out. aussehen / look (outward!). abmachen / agree on (work it off!). English phrasal verbs are not random — they are the same spatial particles German glues on as prefixes. Learn the mirror, not the list.

footnotes.title: The Particle Glossary
footnotes.content: auf = up (wake up, get up, open up). zurück = back (come back, give back). mit = along (take along, bring along). ein = in/into (fall asleep = fall INTO sleep!). aus = out (pick out, look out=appear). an = on (turn on). zu = to/shut (shut-to, like the old 'slam the door to'). ab = off (work off, take off). Eight particles, hundreds of verbs — both languages built from the same eight.

pattern.title: Walk the Wall
pattern.content: The up-row: aufwachen/wake up, aufstehen/get up, aufmachen/open up. The back-row: zurückkommen/come back. The along-row: mitnehmen/take along. The in-row: einschlafen/fall asleep (literally fall INTO sleep). The out-row: aussuchen/pick out, aussehen/look (Du siehst gut aus — you look good OUT). The on-row: anmachen/turn on. The shut-row: zumachen/shut. The off-row: abmachen/agree (work it off — Das ist abgemacht! 'that is off-made' = deal!). Notice anmachen/aufmachen/zumachen all share machen — make — with the particle doing the meaning: German kept make and let the particle steer; English kept make and lost the system.
pattern.linguist_note: English phrasal verbs exploded after 1066 as the native alternative to French/Latin verbs — 'give up' instead of 'surrender'. German never needed the replacement, so its prefixed system stayed intact. The phrasal verbs are English re-Germanizing itself.

exercises.prompt: Mirror wall round one — match the pairs:
exercises.meaning: turn on, shut, pick out, agree on
exercises.explanation: an=on, zu=to/shut, aus=out, ab=off — the same particles as the English phrasal twins.

exercises.prompt: Which particle means UP in German separable verbs?
exercises.explanation: auf is up: wake up, get up, open up — the busiest particle in the mirror wall.

exercises.prompt: 'Du siehst gut aus' — what does 'aus' contribute?
options: The 'look' sense — you look good OUT (outward-facing appearance)
exercises.target_answer: The 'look' sense — you look good OUT (outward-facing appearance)
exercises.explanation: aussehen = look-out: how you look OUTWARD. English 'outlook' kept the same architecture.

exercises.prompt: What is the exact word-for-word German structure of this separable-verb sentence?
exercises.natural: I am getting up early today
options: I am standing up early today
exercises.meaning: I am getting up early today
exercises.explanation: From 'aufstehen' (up-stand): the stem 'stehe' holds position 2 while 'auf' flies to the end of the clause (auf jeden Fall). [Ref: fall asleep]

exercises.prompt: Assemble the German sentence for 'That is a deal (off-made)!':
exercises.meaning: Das ist abgemacht! = That is a deal (off-made)!
exercises.explanation: abmachen's participle: ab + gemacht — the prefix rides the participle. 'It is off-made' — the deal is settled.

summary.outcome: Match fifteen separable verbs to their phrasal twins by particle.
summary.takeaway: Eight particles (auf, zurück, mit, ein, aus, an, zu, ab) run both languages — learn the mirror, not the list.
summary.curiosity_teaser: Next: the Prefix Flight Path — spot the prefix at the sentence end and rebuild with modals.

twist.prompt: Without looking back — build in German: "We wake up here today"
twist.explanation: Building "Wir aufwachen heute hier" from the lesson's core pattern locks in Phrasal Verb Mirrors.

aufwachen.etymology_derivation: Separable: auf (up) + wachen (to be awake/watch); wachen and wake are one verb — a shepherd 'wacht' the flock. [wiktionary]

zurückkommen.shift_rule: T → S / SS / Z + K → CH
zurückkommen.context_translation: We are coming back at eight.
zurückkommen.etymology_derivation: Separable: zu + Rücken (the back, cognate with ridge) + kommen — 'come to-the-back', the exact mirror of come back. [wiktionary]

mitnehmen.context_translation: I want to take the food away / to go.

zumachen.shift_rule: K → CH + T → S / SS / Z

aussuchen.shift_rule: T → S / SS / Z + K → CH
aussuchen.context_phrase: Du kannst dir ein Buch aussuchen.
aussuchen.context_translation: You can choose / seek out a book for yourself.

interessant.etymology_derivation: Borrowed from French interessant; it belongs with Interesse and interessieren, and English interesting grew from the same Latin source, so the two are partners rather than twins. [wiktionary]

nerv.context_phrase: Der Lärm geht mir auf die Nerven.
nerv.context_translation: The noise is getting on my nerves.
nerv.etymology_derivation: From Latin nervus, partly via French nerf. English nerve comes from the same Latin word. [wiktionary]

allein.etymology_derivation: Middle High German al-ein, literally all one — the identical compound that formed English alone (Middle English al-one). [wiktionary]

bank.context_translation: I am going to the bank.
bank.etymology_derivation: The money-changers bench: Bank is the Germanic twin of English bench (Proto-Germanic *bankiz), and the financial sense came through Italian banca. [wiktionary]

rabatt.context_phrase: Heute gibt es zwanzig Prozent Rabatt.
rabatt.context_translation: Today there is twenty percent off.
rabatt.etymology_derivation: From Italian rabbatto via French rabat, from Latin battuere (to beat down); the page documents cognate English rebate — a price beaten down. [wiktionary]

th_to_d.name: The Dental Shift (TH → D)
th_to_d.historical_linguistics: Every single original Germanic "th" sound systematically shifted to "d" in High German, while English kept the ancient "th".
th_to_d.philological_note: Around 500–700 AD in the High German Consonant Shift, dental fricatives hardened into voiced dental stops.

d_to_t.name: The Stop Shift (D → T)
d_to_t.historical_linguistics: Where English kept Germanic "d", High German hardened it into "t".
d_to_t.philological_note: Voiced stops became voiceless. Explains pairs like day ↔ Tag, door ↔ Tür, and drink ↔ trinken.
d_to_t.literature_source: Complementary to the TH → D shift: as TH took over D, original D shifted to T in High German.

p_to_pf_f.name: The Labial Shift (P → PF / F)
p_to_pf_f.historical_linguistics: Proto-Germanic /p/ shifted to the affricate "pf" at the beginning of words, and to "f" or "ff" after vowels.
p_to_pf_f.philological_note: Explains apple ↔ Apfel, pepper ↔ Pfeffer, hope ↔ hoffen, and sleep ↔ schlafen.

t_to_s_ss_z.name: The Sibilant Shift (T → S / SS / Z)
t_to_s_ss_z.historical_linguistics: Proto-Germanic /t/ shifted to sibilant "s/ss/ß" after vowels, and to "z" (/ts/) at the beginning of words.
t_to_s_ss_z.philological_note: Reveals water ↔ Wasser, eat ↔ essen, better ↔ besser, two ↔ zwei, and to ↔ zu.
t_to_s_ss_z.literature_source: Walter Skeat - Primary dental affrication and spirantization

k_to_ch.name: The Velar Shift (K → CH)
k_to_ch.historical_linguistics: Proto-Germanic /k/ softened to the fricative "ch" in medial and final positions.
k_to_ch.philological_note: The Ach-Laut [x] occurs after a, o, u; the Ich-Laut [ç] occurs after e, i, ä, ö, ü.

v_to_b.name: The Bilabial Shift (V / F → B)
v_to_b.historical_linguistics: Intervocalic /v/ and /f/ in English regularly correspond to voiced /b/ in German.
v_to_b.philological_note: Explains give ↔ geben, live ↔ leben, love ↔ lieben, over ↔ über, and seven ↔ sieben.
v_to_b.literature_source: Proto-Germanic bilabial spirant closing to stop in High German

y_gh_to_g_ch.name: The Palatal & Guttural Link (Y → G & GH → CH)
y_gh_to_g_ch.historical_linguistics: English vocalized palatal "g" into "y" (say, day, yesterday) and silenced "gh" (night, laugh, light). German preserved them as "g" or "ch".
y_gh_to_g_ch.philological_note: Explains why English spelling has silent 'gh' letters — they were original German-like gutturals!

latin_ieren.name: The Latin / Romance Layer (-ate / -ize → -ieren)
latin_ieren.phonetic_rule: English verbs ending in -ate, -ize, -ify, -ish ➔ German verbs ending in -ieren
latin_ieren.historical_linguistics: English verbs derived from Latin or French directly map to German verbs ending in -ieren.
latin_ieren.philological_note: Past participles of -ieren verbs never take the "ge-" prefix (studieren → studiert).
latin_ieren.literature_source: Middle High German productive loan suffix from Old French -ier

strong_verbs_ablaut.name: The 7 Strong Verb Classes (Ablaut)
strong_verbs_ablaut.phonetic_rule: English irregular strong verbs with internal vowel changes ➔ German strong verbs following the exact same Ablautreihe
strong_verbs_ablaut.historical_linguistics: Shared 7 Proto-Germanic verb classes where tenses are formed by shifting root vowels.
